item.title: Academic precision
item.description: Precise verbs and adjectives for research, evidence and argument.

children.definition: to support a statement or finding with new evidence from another source
to show that a claim is true by giving evidence for it
children.example: He was unable to substantiate his accusations.

children.definition: to suggest an idea as a basis for an argument or theory
children.example: The author posits that language shapes the way we think.
The link between the two events is tenuous at best.
She summarised the salient points of the report in five minutes.

children.definition: based on observation or experiment rather than theory
children.example: There is little empirical evidence for this claim.

children.definition: to use known facts to estimate or predict something unknown
children.example: It is risky to extrapolate from such a small sample.

children.definition: a warning that something is true only under certain conditions
children.example: The results are encouraging, with one caveat: the trial lasted only six weeks.

children.definition: to wrongly treat two different ideas as if they were the same
children.example: The article conflates correlation with causation.
Smartphones have become ubiquitous in classrooms.

children.definition: a typical model or accepted way of thinking about something
children.example: The discovery led to a paradigm shift in medicine.

children.definition: a difference between two things that should be the same
children.example: There is a discrepancy between the two sets of figures.
